fields.Front: Name the four roles people take on around a DBMS, in one phrase each.
fields.Back:
1. Database Administrator (DBA) - runs the DBMS software
2. Database Designer - identifies the data and builds the model and tables
3. System Analyst / Application Programmer - writes the code that talks to the database
4. End User - uses that software to query and maintain the data

fields.Front: Give at least four responsibilities of a Database Administrator (DBA), and say what a DBA does NOT do.
fields.Back: Give and revoke access; install and upgrade the DBMS; monitor usage; monitor and improve performance (e.g. fix queries running really slowly); check for security violations; back up and restore databases. The DBA runs the software but does NOT create or design the databases.

fields.Front: Describe the Database Designer's job as the sequence the instructor gives.
fields.Back:
1. Collect and identify all the data that must be stored
2. Find the relationships between the data
3. Create a model (the ER diagram)
4. Use the model to create the database and decide what tables are needed
5. Communicate with end users: verify every piece of data is stored, create views, and check they can run efficient queries

fields.Front: Give four responsibilities of a System Analyst / Application Programmer.
fields.Back: Determine the needs of the end users; develop specifications; develop software implementing them in a language that talks to the database; test the implementation; communicate with the end users. In this course: write PHP against a database that already exists.

fields.Front: Give two responsibilities of an End User, the instructor's example query, and when you are an end user in this course.
fields.Back: Generate reports from the database; use the application programmers' software to add, update and query data. Normally an end user does not access the database directly (a standalone user of a small personal Access file might). Example query: 'all the courses taught by Laura Reid.' You are an end user when testing your own software.

fields.Front: Textbook (Elmasri §1.4-1.5): who are the 'actors on the scene' versus the 'workers behind the scene', and what are the four categories of end user?
fields.Back:
ACTORS ON THE SCENE (their daily job involves the data): DBA, database designers, end users, and system analysts and application programmers - the slides' four roles.
WORKERS BEHIND THE SCENE (build and run the software, not interested in the contents): DBMS system designers and implementers (catalog, query processing, concurrency, recovery modules); tool developers (design, performance-monitoring, prototyping and test-data tools, usually bought separately); operators and maintenance personnel.
FOUR END-USER CATEGORIES:
- CASUAL: access occasionally, need different information each time, use a sophisticated query interface (managers).
- NAIVE or PARAMETRIC: constantly query and update through CANNED TRANSACTIONS that were carefully programmed and tested (tellers, reservation agents, receiving clerks).
- SOPHISTICATED: engineers, scientists and analysts who learn most of the DBMS to build their own applications.
- STANDALONE: maintain a personal database through a ready-made package - the instructor's small Access user.

fields.Text: Backing up and restoring the database is the job of the {{c1::DBA}}; creating the data model is the job of the {{c1::database designer}}; writing code against an existing database is the {{c1::application programmer}}; the role that normally does not touch the database directly is the end user.

In this course you take on {{c1::three}} of the four roles - {{c1::database designer, application programmer and end user}} - but not {{c1::DBA}}, because staff have already installed PostgreSQL/MySQL; the code you write is in PHP.
